explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Luke says Jesus "gave them power and authority over all demons" (Luke 9:1). Notice that word "all." He doesn't hand over a little, He hands over authority over every single one.

Nations is a big word, friend, and I see why it tempted you. But the verse never says anything about nations. Jesus gave the Twelve "power and authority over all demons" (Luke 9:1). It's a different kind of authority, and it's the one the text names.

Angels is a fun guess, but the verse doesn't go there. Luke 9:1 says Jesus gave them "power and authority over all demons." Demons, not angels. Easy to mix up when you're moving fast, and I once mixed up salt and sugar, so no judgment here.
That's the one, baker. Luke 9:1 says Jesus gave them authority over all demons "and power to cure diseases." So it's a two-part gift, and both parts come in the same verse.

This one is actually true, friend. The verse says Jesus gave them "power and authority over all demons, and power to cure diseases" (Luke 9:1). Authority over demons is the first part, and power to cure diseases rides right alongside it.
Yes, baker. Jesus "sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick" (Luke 9:2). Two jobs in one sentence. They talk about the kingdom, and they heal the sick.
Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, so I get the pull. But Luke 9:2 says they were sent "to proclaim the kingdom of God." The law of Moses isn't what the verse names as their message.
Nice try, friend, but the temple never comes up in this verse. Jesus sent them "to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick" (Luke 9:2). That's the message, and it's the kingdom.
Careful, baker, this one flips it around. Jesus says, "Take nothing for the journey," and the list includes "no bread, no money" (Luke 9:3). So He tells them to leave both behind, not bring them.

You've got it, friend. Jesus told them, "Take nothing for the journey," and He listed "no bread, no money" right there (Luke 9:3). Bread and money stay home. I would have been checking my pockets twice.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, "Whatever house you enter, stay there until you leave that area" (Luke 9:4). So they stay put in one house instead of hopping around town looking for a nicer one.
That's a very specific number, friend, and I admire the confidence. But Jesus never gives a count of nights. He says to stay in the house "until you leave that area" (Luke 9:4).
The Sabbath is a fair guess, since it's a well-known day on the calendar. But Luke 9:4 doesn't mention it. Jesus says to stay in that house "until you leave that area."

explanations.answer: Shake the dust off their feet
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, "shake the dust off your feet when you leave that town, as a testimony against them" (Luke 9:5). Quiet, simple, and no yelling involved. I think that takes more self-control than I have on a Monday.

explanations.answer: Tear their cloaks at the town gate
explanations.explanation: Tearing cloaks is a dramatic move, friend, but Jesus never says it here. His instruction is, "shake the dust off your feet when you leave that town" (Luke 9:5). Cloaks stay in one piece.

explanations.answer: Call down fire on the town
explanations.explanation: Whoa, friend, that escalated fast. Jesus doesn't tell them to do anything like that. He says, "shake the dust off your feet when you leave that town, as a testimony against them" (Luke 9:5).
You nailed it, baker. Luke says they "went from village to village, preaching the gospel and healing people everywhere" (Luke 9:6). So they're out in the small places, one stop after another.
Jerusalem is a big destination, friend, but this verse doesn't send them there. Luke 9:6 says they "went from village to village." That's a lot of stops, not one straight line.

The text says something different, baker. Luke 9:6 tells us they "went from village to village, preaching the gospel and healing people everywhere." Villages are the stops named, and the word "everywhere" tells you how far it reached.
That's it, baker. Luke 9:7 says Herod "was perplexed." Puzzled and perplexed are twins, and he's scratching his head over all the reports about Jesus.

Pleased isn't what the verse says, friend. Herod the tetrarch, a ruler in Galilee, "was perplexed" when he heard all that was happening (Luke 9:7). Perplexed means puzzled, like staring at a recipe with half the words missing.
Relieved is a reasonable feeling to guess, but it isn't in the text. Luke 9:7 says Herod "was perplexed." He's puzzled, not breathing easy.
Right, baker. Luke 9:8 says some thought "Elijah had appeared." Elijah was a prophet of old, and people were tossing his name into the mix.
Moses is a big name, friend, but he isn't the one in this verse. Luke 9:8 says others thought "Elijah had appeared." Close company, wrong prophet.
Samuel is a good guess, since he was a prophet too. But Luke 9:8 names someone else. It says some were saying "Elijah had appeared."
Yes, baker. Herod says, "I beheaded John, but who is this man I hear such things about?" (Luke 9:9). He's got a pile of rumors and not one clear answer.
Where He comes from is a fair thing to wonder, friend. But it isn't Herod's question in the text. He asks, "who is this man I hear such things about?" (Luke 9:9).
That's a smart question, baker, but it's not the one Herod asks. In Luke 9:9 he says, "who is this man I hear such things about?" His mind is on who Jesus is.
Correct, baker. The passage ends with this line: "And he kept trying to see Jesus" (Luke 9:9). Not once, either. The words "kept trying" tell you he didn't give up.
This one is true, friend. Luke 9:9 closes by saying, "And he kept trying to see Jesus." Herod hears the rumors and keeps trying to see Him for himself.
